column2: Welcome to CoE:RoI!

'Roar of Industry' is the newest edition of 'Concert of Europe' mod. It has initialy been based on PDM, however the whole economy (including pop promotions, etc.) has been majorly overhauled. Aside from that, the mod begins in 1821, and runs up to 1947, which gives you more room to shape the world of your own! There are of course much more changes, too many to list here, so I hope this mod will give you fresh experience!

Slave population remains stable
The slave population in our country has remained just about the same over the year.
Minor growth in Slave population
The slave population in our country has experienced a minor growth over the year.

The slave population in our country has experienced a significant growth over the year.

The slave population in our country has experienced a minor decline over the year.

The slave population in our country has experienced a major decline over the year.
The Republic shall stand under our protection.
Their quarrel is no business of ours.
Our Overlord Demands Their Cores
Our overlord has sent a note demanding that we hand over the provinces they consider rightfully theirs. Refusing would mean war with a power far stronger than our own.
They Accept Our Demands
Our vassal has bowed to our demand and handed over the provinces we claimed. The transfer will be completed within the month.
They Refuse Our Demands
Our vassal has refused to hand over the provinces we claimed, and has done so in terms that leave us no room to retreat.
The Shape of Our Society

A generation after independence the character of our republic is settling. Merchants press for open ports, landowners for order and protection, officers for a larger army, and the clergy for the old certainties. What emerges from this quarrel will shape our nation for decades.
Bad Blood in the Litoral

Our garrisons hold the nitrate provinces, but the Bolivian press calls daily for their return and our own officers speak far too loudly of what they would do to Bolivia if given leave. The affair has become a diplomatic embarrassment.

Washington proclaims that the Americas are closed to European ambition, and presents itself as the guardian of every republic on this continent. Whether that guardianship is a shield or a leash is the question before us.
The Monroe Doctrine
We shall take our place among the modern nations!
The chiefs shall keep their lands and their sovereignty.
Mexico has repudiated the treaties signed after our victory. Their columns are on the march again, and the government in Mexico City denies that any agreement was ever made.
The Second Treaty of Erzurum

The border with the Ottomans has never been drawn on any map both courts would sign, and the tribes of the frontier answer to whichever governor is nearest. British and Russian mediators have proposed a settlement at Erzurum.
The Erzurum Border Commission

The commissioners have completed their survey of the frontier, and their line awards the disputed districts to Persia. The Porte is expected to protest, but the mediating powers have already given their word.
The Goldsmid Arbitration
Expedition into the Great Karoo

Beyond the settled districts of the Cape lies the Karoo, dry and thinly held. A properly funded expedition of surveyors, wagons and troopers could plant permanent settlements at Beaufort, Calvinia and De Aar.
Expedition into Namaqualand
The copper country north of the Cape is known to prospectors but claimed by nobody. A small expedition would be enough to establish a station at Springbok and secure the district.
The Riograndense Republic Stands Alone
The war is over and the flag of the Republic still flies over Piratini. Let us renounce the claims of Rio de Janeiro upon our soil and invite settlers to make their homes among us.
Restore the Spanish Monarchy

The Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis stand before Madrid. With the liberal government broken, we may restore His Most Catholic Majesty to his full authority and end the constitutional experiment in Spain.
Transfer Territory to the Indian Empire
Provinces we hold directly are claimed by our Indian dominion, and administering them from London serves nobody. Let them be placed under the government in Calcutta.
Reverse the Collectivisation of Agriculture

The collective farms have not fed the country as promised. Returning the land to those who work it will please the peasantry and the landowners alike, though the labourers who gained from collectivisation will not forgive it soon.
Galicia and Portugal United
Hide Debug Decisions
Tuck the utility and debug decisions (national value, event toggles, tech school switches) out of sight. They can be brought back at any time.
Show Debug Decisions
Bring the hidden utility and debug decisions back into the decision list.
The Death of Alexander I

The Emperor Alexander, victor over Bonaparte and architect of the Holy Alliance, has died of a fever at Taganrog on the Sea of Azov, far from his capital. St. Petersburg swears allegiance to his brother Constantine in Warsaw, while Warsaw swears allegiance to his brother Nicholas in St. Petersburg. Only a handful of men know that Constantine renounced his rights years ago, in a document sealed away in the Uspensky Cathedral. For three weeks the Empire has two Emperors and obeys neither.
Open the sealed letter and proclaim Nicholas.
The Decembrists on Senate Square

The officers' secret societies have chosen the confusion of the interregnum for their hour. Some three thousand guardsmen stand in square on Senate Square under a grey December sky, shouting for Constantine and for a constitution, most of them believing the two are the same thing. Their chosen dictator has not appeared. Loyal regiments and the guns of the artillery ring the square, and the Emperor waits, still uncrowned, for a decision that will define his reign.
Let the artillery speak. Grapeshot at the square!
Ride out and hear what the officers want.
Then let Constantine have the throne after all.
Revolt in St. Petersburg

Rebellious regiments of the Russian Guard have drawn up in the heart of St. Petersburg, refusing the oath to the new Emperor and demanding a constitution for the Empire. Couriers from the Baltic report the square surrounded by loyal troops and field guns. Every chancellery in Europe is now asking whether the Northern Colossus, the sword of the Holy Alliance, is itself proof against revolution.
Guard regiments have mutinied in St. Petersburg, refusing the oath to the new Emperor and demanding a constitution. Loyal troops and artillery have surrounded them.
Guard regiments mutiny in the Russian capital.
The Third Section

Five conspirators have gone to the gallows and a hundred more to the Siberian mines, but the Emperor has read every word of their testimony and concluded that the rot ran through the best families in the Empire. General Benckendorff proposes a new Third Section of His Majesty's Own Chancellery, with a corps of gendarmes to serve as its hands and eyes in every province. Its business would be nothing less than the opinions of Our subjects.
The Empire shall have its gendarmes.
The ministries and the Church are watch enough.
Pestel's Russian Justice

Colonel Pestel's manuscript, the Russkaya Pravda, has been recovered from the earth where his southern society buried it. It calls for a republic, the abolition of serfdom, and the redistribution of half the land of Russia to the communes. Since the Emperor chose to hear the officers rather than shoot them, no one is quite certain whether the thing is evidence, a petition, or a programme. Printers in both capitals are already setting it in type.
Let it be read and argued over.
Confiscate every copy, quietly.
Nicholaevan Reaction
Riots in Brussels

A performance of Auber's La Muette de Portici at the Theatre de la Monnaie has spilled out into the streets. The crowd has torn the arms of the House of Orange from the shopfronts, the colours of Brabant fly over the Hotel de Ville, and the burghers have armed themselves as a Garde Civique. The southern provinces have grievances enough - Dutch officials, the Dutch language, a Protestant king set over a Catholic people - and the news from Paris has taught them what a crowd may accomplish.
Restore order at the point of the bayonet.
Hear the petitions of the south.
Disorder in Brussels

What began as an evening at the opera has become five days of tumult in the Belgian capital. The Garde Civique patrols the boulevards in place of the royal police, and correspondents report that the tricolour of Brabant has replaced the royal standard on public buildings. Whether The Hague answers with troops or with concessions is the question of the hour in every chancery in Europe.
Brussels is in the hands of an armed citizens' guard after five days of rioting. The Hague has not yet said whether it will send soldiers.
Rioting in Brussels. Royal authority suspended.
The Provisional Government of Belgium

The regiments sent to clear Brussels have been driven out of the Parc after four days of street fighting, and the men of the barricades have proclaimed a Provisional Government. It has declared the southern provinces independent and summoned a National Congress to give them a constitution. His Majesty must now decide whether the Kingdom of the United Netherlands is worth a war, and whether the Powers who assembled it at Vienna will lift a finger to hold it together.
Let them go, and let the Powers settle the rest.
The Kingdom will be preserved by force of arms.
Vienna and Petersburg made this kingdom - let them defend it.
Belgium Declares Its Independence

A Provisional Government sitting in the Hotel de Ville at Brussels has declared the southern provinces of the Kingdom of the United Netherlands to be independent, and has called a National Congress to frame a constitution. The royal troops have withdrawn from the city. The settlement of 1815 has been unmade in a fortnight, and the Powers must decide whether to restore it, recognise the new state, or divide the spoils between them.
A Provisional Government at Brussels has declared the southern provinces independent and summoned a National Congress. The royal troops have withdrawn.
Belgium proclaims independence at Brussels.
The Belgians Appeal to Paris

Envoys of the Provisional Government have arrived in Paris. They speak French, they cheer the tricolour, and they remind the Citizen King that his own throne was raised on barricades only weeks ago. There are deputies in the Chamber who talk again of the natural frontiers, and of a French prince installed at Brussels. There are others who remember that the last time French armies crossed the Scheldt, Europe answered with a coalition.
The Armee du Nord will march for Belgium.
Leave the question to the conference table.
Palmerston and the Belgian Question

The barrier the Powers raised against France in 1815 is coming apart, and the Foreign Secretary must decide what to put in its place. A Belgium in French hands would be intolerable to this country. A Belgium independent, perpetually neutral, and guaranteed by all the Powers together is quite another matter - and the trade of Antwerp would be open to us in either case.
Belgium shall be independent, neutral, and guaranteed.
This is a quarrel for the continent.
The Twenty-Four Articles

The conference has drawn up its terms. Belgium is to be independent and perpetually neutral, the Scheldt is to be opened, the debt of the old kingdom divided, and Limburg and Luxembourg carved between the two crowns. The Powers have set their hands to it. They now expect the King of the Netherlands to do the same, and they have made it plain that the cost of a refusal will not be paid by them.
We will sign, and salvage what we can.
We have not yet been beaten. Let them come.
The Crown of Belgium is Offered

The National Congress has voted for a monarchy and must now find a monarch. The Powers have already vetoed one French prince. Leopold of Saxe-Coburg is a widower of the British royal house, acceptable in London, tolerable in Paris, and beholden to no faction in Brussels. There remain deputies on the benches who would rather have no king at all.
Leopold of Saxe-Coburg shall be King of the Belgians.
Offer the crown to the Duc de Nemours.
Belgium will be a republic.
The Treaty of London, 1839

Nine years of mobilisation have emptied the treasury, and the Powers have not moved an inch from the terms they set in 1831. Belgium is a fact - recognised, garrisoned, and prospering behind its guaranteed neutrality. The Chambers will vote no more money for an army that has done nothing but stand watch at Maastricht. His Majesty may sign, and keep Limburg and half of Luxembourg, or he may go on alone.
Sign. Nine years is long enough.
Not while the Orange flag can still be raised in Brussels.
The Guns Fall Silent

Whatever the terms, the war in the south is over. The regiments are coming back to their depots, the Chambers are counting the cost, and the question of Belgium has passed out of the hands of our generals and into those of the diplomats.
Let the diplomats have it, then.
The London Protocol

On the third of February the plenipotentiaries of Britain, France and Russia signed at London a protocol declaring Greece a fully independent state under the guarantee of the three courts. The protocol settles more than our borders: it settles our form of government, for the powers have resolved that the new state shall be a monarchy under a prince drawn from a neutral house. Leopold of Saxe-Coburg has already declined the offer, and the search for a sovereign continues. The klephts and primates of the Peloponnese, who fought nine years for a free Hellas, are not universally delighted.
Let the powers choose our king.
Greece shall be a republic!
Otto of Wittelsbach Lands at Nafplion

The seventeen-year-old second son of King Ludwig of Bavaria has stepped ashore at Nafplion from a British frigate, greeted by cannon salutes and a crowd that cannot pronounce his name. Being a minor, he does not rule: a regency of three Bavarian councillors governs in his stead, funded by a loan from the guaranteeing powers and protected by three and a half thousand Bavarian troops. They speak no Greek, they distrust the captains of the war, and they intend to build a modern administration whether Hellas wants one or not.
Long live King Othon of the Hellenes.
A Bavarian King for Greece

Prince Otto of Bavaria, not yet eighteen years of age, has landed at Nafplion to assume the crown of the new Kingdom of Greece under the guarantee of Britain, France and Russia. A council of Bavarian regents will govern until his majority, attended by several thousand Bavarian soldiers. Observers in the Levant note that the men who won the war of independence have been given no place in the government of the country they liberated.
Prince Otto of Bavaria has landed at Nafplion to take the Greek crown. A Bavarian regency will govern until he comes of age, backed by Bavarian troops and a loan from the guaranteeing powers.
Otto of Bavaria crowned King of the Hellenes.
The Third of September
Summon the National Assembly.
The crown does not treat with mutineers.
Bavarian Regency

Colonel Kallergis has drawn up the Athens garrison before the palace, and the crowd behind the bayonets is chanting for a constitution. Not a shot has been fired. The King is simply informed that the troops will not disperse until he consents to a national assembly and dismisses the last of his Bavarian advisers, and the guaranteeing powers have signalled that they will not intervene on his behalf.
Monarchy Restored in $COUNTRY$

With parliament deadlocked and the ministries paralysed, the crown of $COUNTRY$ has reclaimed the prerogatives it had ceded. Ministers will henceforth answer to the monarch rather than to the chamber, and the constitution has been rewritten along Prussian lines. Liberals denounce a coup in all but name, while conservatives call it the only remedy to a decade of parliamentary chaos.
The crown of $COUNTRY$ has reclaimed the prerogatives it once ceded to parliament. Ministers now answer to the monarch, and the constitution has been rewritten along Prussian lines.
The monarch of $COUNTRY$ has restored royal rule over parliament.
Unveiled Women Protest in Persia
Commodore Perry has returned from Japan, and the isolation of the islands is at an end.

Dissatisfaction with Portugal's government has grown into open rebellion. The instigator of the first riots is a woman named Maria da Fonte, who led the peasants of the Minho against the prohibition on burials inside churches and against the new taxes. The revolt has spread from village to village, and royal troops sent to restore order have found the countryside against them.
The Catholic Question

Daniel O'Connell has won the by-election in County Clare by a landslide, and as a Catholic he may not take the seat the freeholders have given him. The Catholic Association has forty thousand men under discipline in Ireland and not a shot has been fired. Mr Peel writes to the Duke that the question is no longer whether we shall concede, but whether we shall concede before or after a civil war. The Ultra-Tories answer that the coronation oath binds His Majesty to the Protestant constitution, and that a Parliament opened to Rome is no longer an English Parliament.
Emancipation is the cheaper price
The Protestant constitution stands
The Reform Crisis

Old Sarum returns two members for a green mound. Manchester returns none. Earl Grey's ministry has laid the Reform Bill before the Commons, and the country has taken it up with a violence no ministry expected - the political unions drilling in Birmingham, the papers counting the rotten boroughs by name, and every window in London lit for reform. The Lords have the Bill now. Their lordships may pass it, or they may discover what an unenfranchised nation does when it is told to wait.
Let the Bill pass
The Lords will throw it out
Reform Crisis in Britain

The British Parliament is convulsed by Earl Grey's Reform Bill, which would sweep away the rotten boroughs and give the new manufacturing towns their own members. Crowds gather nightly in Birmingham and London, and the House of Lords must now decide whether to yield or to test the temper of a nation that has just watched Paris unseat a king.
Earl Grey's Reform Bill has reached the House of Lords, and Britain waits in the streets for their lordships' answer.
Britain debates the Reform Bill.
The Days of May

The Lords have wrecked the Bill and the ministry has resigned. The country has answered in a week - placards for 'Go for Gold, to Stop the Duke', a run on the Bank that no chancellor can survive, the Birmingham union promising a hundred thousand men on the road to London, and half the magistrates in the north declining to read the Riot Act to their own neighbours. His Majesty may create as many new peers as are needed to carry the Bill, or the government may hold firm and find out what comes after.
His Majesty will create the peers
We do not legislate under duress
Found the Zollverein

Our tariff law of 1818 swept away the internal customs barriers of the Prussian lands, and the middle states have been drifting into our commercial orbit ever since. Let us now invite every German state outside Vienna's shadow into a single customs union: one tariff, one market, from the Rhine to the Memel. Austria cannot join without dismantling her own protective system, and what begins as a matter of tolls may one day be a matter of crowns.
Form the Southern Customs Union

Berlin's customs union threatens to make the German question an economic one, on ground of Prussia's choosing. Those states that have kept faith with Vienna must not be left to trade at a disadvantage. Let us bind them to our own tariff system instead, and remind Germany that the presidency of the Confederation still sits in the Hofburg.
Zollverein Member
Leader of the Zollverein
Accession to the Zollverein

An embassy has arrived with a draft treaty of accession to the German customs union. Our tolls would be abolished at the frontier, our merchants would trade freely as far as the Baltic, and our share of the common revenue would be paid to us in coin each year. The price is that our tariff policy would no longer be our own, and that Vienna would read our signature as a defection.
Sign the treaty of accession
Our customs are our sovereignty
A German Customs Union Is Proposed

Delegates from the German states have been summoned to consider a treaty abolishing internal tariffs across much of the Confederation. The union would create a single market of some twenty-five million people, with a common external tariff and revenues divided by population. Observers in Vienna have received the news coldly, noting that the Austrian protective system makes accession impossible for the imperial government.
A treaty abolishing internal German tariffs has been laid before the middle states. Vienna cannot accede without abandoning its own protective system.
German states weigh a common customs union.
A German State Accedes

The treaty of accession has been signed and the customs posts on that frontier are to be taken down within the year. Every state that joins makes the next accession easier, for the holdouts find themselves ringed by a market they cannot enter on equal terms.
One tariff, one Germany
A German State Stays Out

Our embassy has returned empty-handed. The court in question prefers its own tolls, its own bridge dues and the goodwill of Vienna to a share of our common revenue. It may yet be brought round by patience, or by the simple arithmetic of being left outside.
Let them count the cost of exclusion
Offer better terms and keep talking
Berlin's Customs Union

Reports from our envoys in the smaller courts are unanimous: Prussia is assembling a commercial union across Germany that we cannot join without dismantling the protective tariffs on which our own industry depends. Prince Metternich observes that the Confederation was built to contain exactly this, and that a union of tolls will not stop at tolls.
Hold the loyal courts by other means
Denounce this breach of the Confederation
The German Customs Union Is Complete

On the first of January the barriers came down. Thirty-eight tariff frontiers, with their gaugers and their toll-houses and their thirty-eight schedules of duties, have been reduced to one. Goods now travel from the Rhine to the eastern provinces without inspection, weights and measures are being brought into line, and the states that stayed outside are already asking on what terms they might be admitted. We did not set out to unify Germany. We may have begun to.
The barriers are down
The Customs Barriers Come Down

At midnight the chains were lifted at the internal frontiers of the German customs union and long files of waggons, which had been drawn up on the roads since the previous evening, passed through without inspection. Merchants describe the change as the greatest single alteration to German trade in living memory. Political observers are less sanguine: a union of tariffs, they note, has a way of becoming a union of something else.
The internal tariff frontiers of the German customs union were lifted at midnight, creating a single market across most of the Confederation.
German internal tariffs abolished at midnight.
The Eskinci Corps
Turn the guns on the barracks!
Let the kettles lie.
Cannon in the Etmeydani

Constantinople is under martial law after the destruction of the Janissary corps. Reports reaching Vienna describe the guns of the Sultan's artillery firing upon the Janissary barracks at close range until the buildings were alight, and the survivors hunted through the quarters of the city for three days. The corps that once carried the Ottoman standard to the walls of Vienna has been abolished by imperial edict, its name forbidden, its dervish protectors banished. The Porte styles the affair the Auspicious Incident. Whether the Sultan can now conjure a modern army from the ashes of the old is the question every chancellery in Europe is asking.
The Sultan's artillery has destroyed the Janissary corps in its Constantinople barracks. The order is abolished by edict and its name forbidden. The Porte calls the affair the Auspicious Incident.
The Janissary corps is destroyed by cannon in Constantinople.
The Mansure Army

The Janissaries are gone and with them the greater part of the army's officers, its drill, and its supply. What remains is the Asakir-i Mansure-i Muhammediye - the Victorious Soldiers of Muhammad - a paper establishment that must be turned into regiments before the next war finds us. Uniforms have been ordered, barracks are building, and the treasury groans. The one thing that cannot be bought in the bazaar is instruction.
Engage Prussian and French instructors.
Send to Egypt for officers.
A Second Reckoning
Strike now, before it is too late.
The corps has earned its place.
New Order Army
Janissary Ascendancy
The Organic Statute
Abolish the Kingdom's separate institutions.
Restore the charter and rule by conciliation.

Sultan Mahmud II has spent a decade waiting. The Janissary corps, once the terror of Christendom, has become a corporation of shopkeepers and street bullies that has deposed three sultans and butchered a fourth. On the fourteenth of June the Sultan proclaims the Eskinci - a new corps of picked men to be drilled, uniformed and paid in the European manner. Within two days the Janissaries of Istanbul have overturned their soup kettles in the Etmeydani, the ancient signal of mutiny, and the crowd is calling for the heads of the Sultan's ministers. Loyal artillery stands ready in the Hippodrome, and the Sheikh ul-Islam has been sounded out for a fetva. The Sultan must decide whether this is the reckoning at last.

Five years have passed since the Sultan drew back from the Etmeydani, and the corps has not grown more tractable for the reprieve. The aghas sit in the divan as though they had won a battle. Every proposal for a new levy dies in committee, and the provinces take their cue from the capital. The Sultan's ministers argue that what was possible in 1826 is still possible now, and that it will not be possible for much longer.

The Polish rising is broken. Warsaw has fallen, the Sejm that dared depose the Tsar is scattered across Prussia and Galicia, and thousands of officers and gentry have taken the road to Paris rather than the road home. What remains is to settle what the Kingdom of Poland shall be. The Constitution of 1815 gave the Poles their own Sejm, their own army and their own coinage under the Tsar's crown, and His Majesty's advisers are unanimous that it gave them the means of the rebellion as well. An Organic Statute has been drafted that would replace the constitution altogether, abolishing the Sejm and the Polish army and administering the Kingdom as a Russian province in all but name.
The Constitutional Charter and Dom Miguel's Return

Dom Pedro has sent us a Constitutional Charter from Rio and abdicated the Portuguese crown in favour of his infant daughter, Maria da Gloria. His brother Dom Miguel is to return from exile in Vienna, swear the Charter and rule as regent in her name. Instead, from the moment he lands at Lisbon the absolutists have thronged the palace, the Cortes has been dissolved, and the municipalities are being made to acclaim him king in his own right. The garrison of Oporto and the officers of the Azores refuse to read the proclamation.
Long live King Miguel I, absolute lord of Portugal!
The Cortes will not surrender the Charter.
Dom Miguel Acclaimed King in Lisbon

Dom Miguel, returned from exile to serve as regent for his niece, has been acclaimed absolute king by the assembled estates in Lisbon. The Constitutional Charter is set aside, the Cortes dissolved and the liberal deputies scattered. The northern garrisons and the Azores have not submitted, and London has recalled its minister.
The estates in Lisbon have acclaimed Dom Miguel absolute king. The Charter is set aside and the north has not submitted.
Dom Miguel acclaimed absolute king.
The Liberals at Terceira

The Charter's defenders have not been extinguished. A regency in the name of Queen Maria sits at Angra on Terceira, the emigration in London and Plymouth drills openly, and the Azorean squadron flies the constitutional colours. Dom Pedro, having abdicated in Brazil, is said to be gathering ships and money to land in the north. Oporto has always been a liberal city, and it is watching the sea.
Blockade the islands and purge the north.
Let the exiles rot in their Atlantic rock.
The Convention of Evora Monte

After the landing at Mindelo, the siege of Oporto and the loss of the fleet off Cape St Vincent, the war of the two brothers has burned itself out. Both armies are ragged, the treasury is empty and the powers have made it plain that they will not tolerate another year of it. Envoys are meeting at Evora Monte to settle the succession once and for all.
Miguel shall abdicate and go into exile. The Charter is restored.
No convention. The King holds Portugal, whatever Europe says.
Peace at Evora Monte Ends the War of the Brothers

The convention signed at Evora Monte closes the Portuguese civil war. Dom Miguel renounces every claim to the crown and leaves the kingdom on a pension, Queen Maria II is restored under the Constitutional Charter, and the emigration returns to Lisbon. The Quadruple Alliance has its settlement and Britain her ally on the Tagus.
The convention of Evora Monte ends the Portuguese civil war: Miguel renounces the crown and the Charter is restored under Queen Maria II.
Evora Monte ends the Portuguese civil war.
The Miguelite Revolt

The Cortes has kept the Charter, but the King's brother has not gone quietly. Absolutist bands are up in Tras-os-Montes and the Alentejo under the cry of 'King Miguel and the Holy Faith', friars preach against the constitution from every pulpit, and whole regiments have gone over to the pretender. The loyalty of the army is now the whole question.
The Charter holds. Scatter them.
The army has declared for Miguel. It is over.
The Monroe Doctrine
America for the Americans!
The Old World is no concern of ours
The Tariff of Abominations
Sign the bill
Strike out the higher schedule
The Nullification Crisis
The Force Bill in one hand, Clay's compromise in the other
March the army into Charleston
South Carolina Nullifies the Tariff
Tariff of Abominations
Sectional Tension

In his annual message to Congress, President Monroe has set out a principle for the whole hemisphere. The American continents are no longer open to European colonisation, and any attempt by the powers of the Holy Alliance to extend their system to the new republics would be regarded as dangerous to our peace and safety. In return we pledge not to meddle in the wars of Europe. Canning's Britain would welcome such a declaration. Metternich will call it insolence.

The tariff bill that has come out of committee raises duties on raw wool, hemp, iron and molasses to rates no manufacturer ever asked for. New England mills are protected. The cotton planters of the South, who buy in a protected market and sell in a free one, call it a tariff of abominations and say plainly that it taxes them for the benefit of Northern industry. Vice President Calhoun is said to be drafting an Exposition against it.

A convention at Columbia has declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null and void within South Carolina, forbidden the collection of duties in Charleston after February, and threatened secession should force be used. President Jackson answers that disunion by armed force is treason, and asks Congress for a Force Bill. In the same breath Henry Clay offers a compromise tariff falling by degrees over ten years. The Union has never been tested in this manner.
Let the tariff die - the Union is worth more

A state convention at Columbia has pronounced the federal tariffs of 1828 and 1832 unauthorised by the Constitution and void within South Carolina, and has forbidden the collection of duties at Charleston. The President has replied that the laws of the Union will be executed, and has asked Congress for authority to use the army and navy. Senator Clay meanwhile lays before the chamber a tariff descending by stages over ten years. Whether the quarrel ends in a compromise or in the first use of federal arms against a state is the question of the hour in every counting-house from Boston to New Orleans.

South Carolina has declared the federal tariff void within her borders and forbidden its collection at Charleston. The President demands a Force Bill, while Senator Clay offers a compromise schedule instead.
South Carolina declares the tariff void. The President asks for a Force Bill.
Diponegoro's Rising

Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta has raised the green banner of holy war. A road driven through his ancestral graves at Tegalreja was the spark, but the grievance is older - the land rents, the toll gates and the Resident's tutelage over the courts of Java. Regents, santri and peasants are flocking to him, and our garrisons in the interior are too few and too scattered to hold the passes.
General de Kock will pacify the interior.
Buy off the princes before the island burns.
We are stretched too thin in Europe to fight in Asia.
Holy War Proclaimed in Java

A prince of the house of Yogyakarta has proclaimed a holy war against the Dutch in central Java. Reports from Batavia speak of the interior in flames, of Netherlands columns ambushed on the mountain roads, and of the old regents deserting to the rebel camp.
A Javanese prince has proclaimed a holy war against the Dutch, and the interior of the island is in flames.
Java rises against the Dutch.
Diponegoro Captured at Magelang

Five years of guerrilla war, the benteng-stelsel of fortified posts and the slow starvation of the rebel districts have ended the rising. Invited to Magelang under a flag of truce to negotiate, Diponegoro was seized and is to be exiled to Celebes. The victory has cost us fifteen thousand soldiers and a treasury we no longer have. Java is quiet, ruined and must now be made to pay.
Van den Bosch shall introduce the Cultivation System.
Java must be governed with a lighter hand.
The Java War Is Over

The rebel prince of Yogyakarta has been taken at Magelang, having come to the Dutch camp under a flag of truce, and is to be carried into exile in the eastern islands. Five years of war in the interior are said to have cost the Netherlands fifteen thousand soldiers and the greater part of the colonial revenue.
The rebel prince of Yogyakarta has been taken at Magelang and exiled. The Java War is over.
The Java War ends in Dutch victory.
The Bargain with the Regents

Rather than march into the mountains we have gone to the courts with money. The land rents of the princely districts are remitted, the toll gates on the Progo are pulled down, and the regents keep their apanages and their dignity. Diponegoro's following melts away before it can become an army. The Indies will earn us less for some years - but they will not cost us an army either.
A cheap peace is still a peace.
Java War
Cultivation System
The Carbonari
Watch the lodges, and do not make martyrs.
Break them. Arrests, and the galleys.
Ciro Menotti's Conspiracy

Ciro Menotti of Carpi has been meeting our Duke in private for a year, dangling before him a crown: let Francesco IV put himself at the head of a rising, and a united Italy of the north might be his. Paris has driven out its Bourbon and the news has emboldened every liberal from Turin to Bologna. Now Menotti's men are arming in a house on the Via Grande, and the Duke must decide whether he is their patron or their gaoler.
Surround the house. Menotti hangs.
Hesitate - and let the rising come.
Revolt in the Legations

Bologna has risen. The papal legate was put in a carriage and sent north, the tricolour flies over the Palazzo d'Accursio, and an assembly has proclaimed the United Italian Provinces, declaring the temporal power of the Holy See at an end. Ferrara, Ravenna and Ancona have followed within the week, and the whole of the Romagna is lost to us. Rome has no army worth the name. Austria has a corps at Ferrara and Vienna needs only to be asked.
Ask Vienna to restore order.
Concede: a lay administration and reform.
BOLOGNA PROCLAIMS THE UNITED ITALIAN PROVINCES

An assembly at Bologna has declared the temporal power of the Pope at an end and proclaimed the United Italian Provinces. The papal legate has been escorted from the city and the revolt has carried Ferrara, Ravenna and Ancona with it. Correspondents report that the Holy See, possessing no field army, has turned its eyes to the Austrian garrisons north of the Po.
The Legations have risen against the Holy See and proclaimed the United Italian Provinces at Bologna. Rome has no army to send against them.
The Papal Legations are in revolt.

Charcoal-burners, they call themselves, and their lodges have spread from the Abruzzi into every city of the peninsula. The vendite meet by night, swear their oaths on daggers, and pass tracts calling for a constitution and for Italy. Naples and Turin rose on their word in 1820 and 1821, and Austrian bayonets put both risings down - the lodges themselves were never broken. Our police know the names of half their leaders. The question is what we mean to do with them.
The Austrian Intervention

The Holy Father has asked for our troops. Prince Metternich reminds the Council that Troppau and Laibach bound the powers to put down revolution wherever it raises its head, and that we did precisely this at Naples and at Turin ten years ago. General Frimont's corps can be over the Po in a fortnight and in Bologna before the rebels have found a general. France, however, has a citizen king who has proclaimed the principle of non-intervention, and Paris will not be silent.
Frimont will cross the Po.
Let it burn. We will not be Europe's gendarme.
AUSTRIAN COLUMNS CROSS THE PO

At the request of the Holy See, Austrian troops have entered the Papal Legations to put down the revolt of the United Italian Provinces. Vienna justifies the march by the principles agreed at Troppau and Laibach, under which the powers undertook to suppress revolution in the states of Italy. The cabinets of Paris and London have been informed rather than consulted.
Austrian troops have entered the Papal Legations at the request of Rome, invoking the Troppau principles against the Bolognese revolt.
Austria marches into the Legations.
The Powers and the Legations

The Italian question is on every desk in Europe. Vienna claims a right of intervention in the peninsula that no treaty of 1815 ever wrote down, and the courts must decide whether to say so aloud. Our ambassador wants instructions: a note of protest and a memorandum demanding reform of the papal administration, or a polite silence that leaves Italy to Austria as the price of quiet elsewhere.
Protest, and demand reform in the Legations.
Say nothing. Italy is Austria's affair.
THE CABINETS AND THE ITALIAN QUESTION

The revolt in the Papal Legations has put the Italian question before every cabinet in Europe. At issue is whether Austria may act as the police of the peninsula on the invitation of any prince who asks, and whether the powers who signed at Vienna in 1815 have anything to say about how the Holy See governs its subjects.
The powers weigh a protest against Austrian intervention in Italy, and a memorandum on the government of the Papal Legations.
Europe debates the Italian question.
The Schleswig-Holstein Question Resolved
The Daoguang Edicts
Let the edicts be proclaimed and obeyed!
The Canton trade pays for itself.
The Silver Drain
Debase the coinage and be done with it.
Send a High Commissioner to Canton!
Legalise the drug and take our duty on it.
The Canton Trade

Word reaches London that the Emperor has renewed the prohibition of opium and means it this time. The Company's monopoly is dead, the free traders of Jardine and Matheson are loud in Parliament, and the Indian revenue leans heavily on the drug. The Superintendent at Canton asks for instructions, and behind him the merchants ask for frigates.
The trade must go on - and be protected.
We shall respect the edicts of the Emperor.
Opium Prohibition
The Canton Squeeze
Silver Drain

The new Emperor has scarcely been enthroned before the censors lay before him a mountain of memorials on the foreign drug. Opium chests land at Lintin by the thousand, paid for in Spanish silver that never returns, and magistrates, customs officers and the Hong merchants alike take their cut of the traffic. The Son of Heaven may thunder against the poison, or he may quietly acknowledge what every official at Canton already knows.

For a decade the edicts have been read aloud and ignored. The exchange rate of copper cash to silver has collapsed, taxes assessed in silver ruin the peasantry, and the treasury of the Board of Revenue empties into the holds of foreign clippers. Huang Juezi demands death for the smoker, while others urge that the trade be legalised, taxed, and paid for in tea rather than bullion.
The Tsar's Ultimatum
Cross the Prut - the army marches on the Danube!
Press the Porte at the conference table.
The Treaty of Adrianople

Diebitsch has crossed the Balkan range and stands at Adrianople, two days' march from Constantinople itself. The Sultan's envoys sue for terms. Nesselrode counsels moderation: a weak Ottoman Empire on the Straits serves us better than a scramble among the powers over its corpse. The Danubian principalities can be placed under our protection, the Serbs granted their privileges, Greek freedom recognised - or the army can march on the capital and take the prize outright, whatever London and Vienna may say.
Moderation. Sign the peace at Adrianople.
The road to Constantinople is open.
The Powers and the Straits

Russian columns are on the road to Constantinople and no Ottoman army stands between them and the Bosphorus. Should the Tsar seat himself astride the Straits, the balance of Europe settled at Vienna is undone at a stroke, and the road to the Mediterranean lies open to the Russian fleet. Our ambassadors must decide whether a note of protest suffices, or whether the Sultan is to be propped up with more than words.
A formal protest will be lodged.
The Porte must be sustained.
The Peace of Adrianople

The infidel armies stood at Adrianople and the capital was defenceless, yet the Tsar has offered terms rather than the sword. We must yield the mouth of the Danube and the Georgian fortresses, open the Straits to Russian commerce, confirm the privileges of the principalities and of the Serbs, and abandon the Greek provinces. The Empire survives, humbled, and the reforms of our late army can no longer be delayed.
The Empire endures. We shall rebuild.

The Porte has flouted the Convention of Akkerman, closed the Straits to our merchantmen and answered the protocols of the powers with silence. Since the allied fleets destroyed the Ottoman navy at Navarino the Sultan has proclaimed a holy war against us and disavowed every article we signed. Wittgenstein's armies stand ready on the Prut, and the principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia would welcome them as liberators. The Greeks look to Saint Petersburg, and so does the whole of the Orthodox world.
MacCarthy's Expedition

Since the Crown took the African Company's forts into its own hands, Ashanti claims over the Fante states have pressed hard upon the Gold Coast. Sir Charles MacCarthy, Governor at Cape Coast, is convinced that a single show of force will settle the question, and would march inland with the militia and what allies the coast will furnish. The Asantehene's army is reckoned in tens of thousands.
March on Kumasi
Hold the coast and the forts
Disaster at Nsamankow
Avenge the Governor
Peace on the Pra

Since the field of Dodowa the Asantehene's army has kept behind the Pra, and neither side gains by another season in the bush. The traders want a boundary they can name, the Fante states want a guarantee, and Whitehall wants the Gold Coast off the estimates. A treaty fixing the Pra as the frontier, with the coastal states left outside Ashanti authority, is within reach.
Fix the boundary on the Pra
Press on to Kumasi
The Golden Stool Stands

The white governor's column has been swallowed whole in the forest, and his head is borne to Kumasi. The Asantehene's authority over the interior is confirmed before every tributary chief, and the coastal states must reckon again with whom they deal.
The Golden Stool stands
Governor MacCarthy Killed on the Gold Coast

News has reached the coast of the destruction of Sir Charles MacCarthy's column at Nsamankow. The Governor is dead, the militia scattered, and the Ashanti army stands between the forts and the interior. The merchants of Cape Coast petition for regular troops.
Sir Charles MacCarthy's column has been destroyed at Nsamankow and the Governor is dead. The Gold Coast forts stand exposed.
MacCarthy killed at Nsamankow.

At Nsamankow on the Bonsa the Governor's small column was surrounded, its ammunition reserve found to hold the wrong stores, and destroyed. Sir Charles MacCarthy is dead, and his skull is carried to Kumasi as a war trophy. The coast is in a panic and the merchants of Cape Coast are writing to London for regular troops.
